title: Man shot by RCMP feared the police: U.S. squatter thought officers would try to deport him again, friend says
article: Donald Dwayne Lewis, the 43-year-old man shot dead by a Williams Lake RCMP officer on Aug. 13, left his home in Whistler a few weeks ago because he was illegally in Canada and afraid police in the resort town would try to deport him again, according to one of Lewis's close friends.
"He just thought the cops were going to hassle him in Whistler so he wasn't staying there," said Leigh Wilson, who said he had known Lewis for about a decade.
Lewis was shot in what RCMP are calling a "violent struggle" after a lone RCMP officer responded to a report of a man camping illegally near McLeese Lake, off Highway 97.
The officer, who had been on the force for about a year, suffered a broken hand and injuries to his head.
Wilson said Lewis had been living for many years in a self-built shack in the woods around Whistler.
A U.S. citizen without legal status here, he had been deported at least four times -- most recently in February 2006.
A month after that most recent deportation, said Wilson, Lewis reappeared in Whistler.
"I guess he snuck across the border," said Wilson.
Lewis was becoming increasingly worried that he was too much of a target in Whistler, said Wilson, and that it would only be a matter of time before he was deported again.
So, despite marrying his girlfriend of seven years just last year, Lewis decided to skip town.
Wilson said he saw Lewis driving a motorcycle about a month ago and lent him a sleeping bag for his journey north. Living outdoors was nothing new for Lewis.
In a resort community known for its million-dollar condos, Lewis lived as a squatter in the woods.
"He was kind of a hermit," said Wilson.
Off an isolated gravel logging road, Lewis built a shack made in part from an old, dilapidated van.

"It's nothing fancy, that's for sure, but it was a roof over his head," said Wilson. "He had a generator and some electricity and some water close by. And in the winter time he had to shovel a lot of snow to get in and out."
What little money Lewis needed, said Wilson, he made by doing odd jobs in town and selling cords of firewood he cut out of the woods.
A year ago he married his longtime girlfriend, Sarah Penny, who lives in Pemberton.
But they disagreed over where they should live.
She wanted him to move in with her and her children, said Wilson, but "he wanted her to come and live in the squat with him."
A message left for Penny was not returned.
Wilson said Lewis was a deeply religious man.
"He walked around with a Bible and quoted scripture," he said.
Tim Unruh, pastor at the Whistler Community Church, said Lewis attended service there sporadically.
"Don and I had several conversations," said Unruh. "Don spoke easily of spiritual things."

Asked what he thought when he heard Lewis had been shot by the police, Unruh replied: "I wasn't surprised when I heard it . . . When someone is shot, that's a tragic event. But, no, I can't say that I was really surprised."
Unruh refused to elaborate on what he meant, other than to say he wished Lewis had made different choices in his life.
"I think Don in his heart, he trusted Jesus," he said. "I think sometimes he just made some choices that had hard consequences."
In June 2005, Lewis was charged with assaulting Whistler RCMP Const. Chris Palmquist, who was trying to arrest him on an immigration warrant.
He pleaded guilty and served 21 days in jail.
Wilson said Lewis told him he didn't realize the man arresting him was a police officer.
"He just thought someone was attacking him. So he struggled to get free," said Wilson.
However, Arlene Loyst, the Crown prosecutor who handled the case, said Palmquist had arrested Lewis once before -- in May 2004 -- on another immigration warrant.
And, according to Palmquist's report on the incident, said Loyst, "as the officer approached Lewis, he immediately said, 'I'm not going.'"
Police have released few details about Sunday's shooting, but Wilson said he has trouble believing Lewis could have attacked the officer.
"In 10 years of knowing him, I didn't see him doing anything aggressive," said Wilson.
He also said Lewis never did drugs and rarely drank.
Lewis's mother Darlene Sabatelli, who lives in Iowa, said her son wasn't violent.
"He was a Christian. He was fun-loving," she said. "He wouldn't hurt a fly unless someone was trying to cross him or hurt him."
Wilson said he also doubts Lewis -- whom he described as 5'3" (160 centimetres) tall and weighing 130 pounds (59 kilograms)-- would pose much of a threat.
"I'm sure I could subdue Don without shooting him," he said.
The RCMP has refused to comment further on the shooting, which is now being investigated by Delta police.
